Source paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Source paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Source paper year of publication: 2024
Related papers: 
1. Title: Fine-Tuning CLIP Models with Convolutional Features for Medical Anomaly Detection
   Abstract: Despite the significant success of large-scale vision-language pre-training models in zero-shot and few-shot anomaly detection for natural images, their effectiveness is sharply limited in the medical domain by the substantial discrepancy between natural and medical image data. To address this domain shift, This study presents a new, lightweight framework named Multi-Level Convolution Adaptation (MLCA), which is designed for medical anomaly detection by fine-tune the CLIP model. Our methodology enhances the pre-trained visual encoder by integrating multiple residual adapters to progressively refine visual features across various layers. Furthermore, we implement a ConvTokenizer to align CLIP’s image tokens directly with the raw input information, thereby preserving critical original details. This adaptation process is rigorously supervised by a pixel-level visual-text alignment loss function, which deliberately recalibrates the model’s attention away from recognizing object semantics towards the accurate recognition of anomalies in medical images. The resulting adapted features exhibit markedly enhanced generalization across diverse medical data types, yielding promising zero-shot capabilities even when the model engagement sentirely novel medical modalities or underexplored anatomical regions during inference. Experimental validation on standard MAD benchmarks confirms that MLCA surpasses existing SOTA models, showing the average value of AUC improvement of 2.44% and 1.18% for anomaly classification under zero-shot and few-shot conditions, respectively, and corresponding average AUC gains of 1.33% and 0.57% for anomaly segmentation.
   Year: 2025

Research problem the idea must address (selected in an earlier step):
In MVFA's zero-shot (leave-one-modality-out) training, the segmentation adapters — the only part that produces anomaly maps — are trained with Dice and Focal losses exclusively on the three source datasets that have pixel masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), while OCT17, ChestXray and HIS only train the detection adapters. Primary question: can the segmentation adapters be trained from image-level labels alone, and how much mask-supervised localisation does that retain on the unseen modality? At each of the four adapter levels, with the original level weights, the Dice and Focal terms are replaced by an image-level BCE on the top-k mean of the level's patch-to-text anomaly probabilities (k = 1% of patches), applied to all five source datasets with every mask discarded; the detection adapters and their loss are unchanged. Hypothesis: because patch scores are similarities to text anchors shared by all modalities, this weak supervision yields localisation that transfers to the unseen modality. Primary outcomes: pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO on the held-out folds with masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) and image-level AUROC on all folds, mask-supervised versus image-label-supervised MVFA under the shared protocol. Secondary analyses: (i) a control in which the text anchors of the segmentation branch are replaced by a learned linear patch classifier trained with the same MIL loss, isolating the role of the text anchors; (ii) a per-level breakdown; (iii) two label-budget points with masks for 10% and 25% of the abnormal source images (one seed, two folds).

Code-verified facts about the public code of the source paper (github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD):
- CLIP/adapter.py: CLIP_Inplanted wraps a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14-336 (input 240x240); ClipAdapter bottleneck adapters are inserted after layers [6, 12, 18, 24]; there are two adapter sets, seg_adapters (segmentation branch) and det_adapters (detection branch), mixed residually with ratio 0.1.
- prompt.py / utils.py: the text side is two frozen text anchors (normal, abnormal) averaged over 35 templates.
- train_zero.py (zero-shot, leave-one-dataset-out): det branch trained with BCE on the MEAN-pooled patch anomaly map for every image; seg branch trained with Focal + Dice on pixel masks only for BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC; batch size 1; the checkpoint is selected on the target test set.
- train_few.py: few-shot fine-tuning on K normal + K abnormal (masked) images from BMAD's valid/ split, one fixed draw (dataset/fewshot_seed); the checkpoint is selected on the target test set.
- test_few.py: zero-shot map (text similarity) and few-shot map (1 - max cosine to a memory bank of support patch features, per level) are each min-max normalised over the whole test set and added with weight 0.5; image score = max of fused pixel map (masked datasets) or mean-pooled det score (others).
- BMAD: BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC have masks; OCT17, ChestXray, HIS have image labels only; each has train/valid/test splits.

Required evaluation protocol: Shared evaluation protocol (from the limitation group 'Leakage-free generalisation protocol': L1, L2, L11, L20, L22, L27, L37, C2): checkpoints and hyper-parameters are selected on a held-out validation split of the SOURCE modalities and never on the target test set, and the MVFA baseline is re-run under the same rule; results are reported under a modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out split (RESC and OCT17 are held out together, never one with the other in training), with patient-level separation where identifiers exist, over at least 3 random seeds and 3 few-shot support draws with mean and standard deviation, and with a simple supervised baseline trained on the same labelled images (L31) where relevant.
